function.name: generate_report
function.description: Generates a comprehensive report based on user activity data within a specified time frame. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

user_id.description: The unique identifier for the user.

start_date.description: The start date for the report period in the format 'YYYY-MM-DD'.

end_date.description: The end date for the report period, inclusive, in the format 'YYYY-MM-DD'.

include_inactive.description: Flag to determine if inactive users should be included in the report.

report_format.description: The format in which the report will be generated.

message.content:
**Choosing the “best” ionisation method depends on what you’re trying to analyse and the constraints of your experiment.** Below is a quick guide to help you decide which ionisation technique might suit your needs best. | Ionisation Method | Typical Applications | Advantages | Disadvantages | When to Use | |-------------------|----------------------|------------|---------------|-------------| | **Electron Impact (EI)** | Small, volatile, thermally stable molecules (e.g., hydrocarbons, pesticides). | • Simple, robust;
• Produces reproducible fragmentation patterns;
• Good for library matching. | • Requires gas‑phase molecules;
• Not suitable for large, labile biomolecules. | When you need a standard, high‑throughput analysis of small organic compounds. | | **Chemical Ionisation (CI)** | Semi‑volatile organics, pharmaceuticals, environmental contaminants. | • Softer than EI;
• Produces [M+H]+ or [M+Na]+ ions;
• Lower background noise. | • Requires a reagent gas;
• Less reproducible fragmentation. | When you need a softer ionisation for compounds that fragment too much under EI. | | **Electrospray Ionisation (ESI)** | Proteins, peptides, nucleic acids, large biomolecules, metabolites. | • Very soft;
• Produces multiply charged ions, reducing m/z range;
• Compatible with LC‑MS. | • Requires a liquid sample;
• Susceptible to ion suppression. | When analysing large, polar, or thermally labile molecules. | | **Atmospheric Pressure Chemical Ionisation (APCI)** | Small to medium‑size, moderately polar molecules (e.g., drugs, steroids). | • Works with LC‑MS;
• Handles less polar compounds than ESI. | • Less effective for highly polar analytes. | When you need a hybrid between ESI and GC‑MS for LC‑MS. | | **Matrix‑Assisted Laser Desorption/Ionisation (MALDI)** | Proteins, peptides, polymers, large biomolecules. | • Very soft;
• High throughput;
• Minimal fragmentation. | • Requires matrix;
• Limited to solid samples. | When you need rapid screening of large biomolecules or polymers. | | **Laser Desorption Ionisation (LDI)** | Biomolecules without a matrix (e.g., sugars, lipids). | • No matrix needed;
• Useful for imaging. | • Often produces lower ion yields. | When you want to avoid matrix interference. | | **Field‑Ionisation (FII)** | Small, volatile molecules; high‑resolution MS. | • Extremely soft;
• Produces singly charged ions. | • Requires high vacuum;
• Limited to small molecules. | When you need ultra‑soft ionisation for small molecules. | | **Atmospheric Pressure Photoionisation (APPI)** | Non‑polar, aromatic compounds, PAHs. | • Works with non‑polar analytes;
• Compatible with LC‑MS. | • Requires a photoioniser;
• Less common. | When analysing non‑polar, aromatic compounds that are difficult for ESI/APCI. | ### How to pick 1. **Sample type & size** - *Small, volatile*: EI or CI. - *Large, polar, labile*: ESI or MALDI. - *Non‑polar aromatics*: APPI. 2. **Desired ionisation softness** - *Hard ionisation* (fragmentation): EI. - *Soft ionisation* (intact ions): ESI, MALDI, FII. 3. **Instrument compatibility** - *GC‑MS*: EI, CI. - *LC‑MS*: ESI, APCI, APPI. - *TOF‑MS imaging*: MALDI, LDI. 4. **Throughput & reproducibility** - EI and CI are highly reproducible and ideal for library matching. - ESI and MALDI offer high throughput but may need optimisation for ion suppression. 5. **Matrix effects** - ESI is prone to ion suppression; consider using APCI or APPI if matrix effects are severe. ### Quick decision tree ``` ┌─ Is the analyte small (< 500 Da) and volatile? ──► EI (hard) or CI (soft) │ ├─ Is the analyte large (> 500 Da) or polar? ──► ESI (soft) or MALDI (soft) │ ├─ Is the analyte non‑polar aromatic? ──► APPI (soft) │ └─ Need high‑throughput imaging? ──► MALDI or LDI ``` --- **Bottom line:** - For routine small‑molecule analysis in GC‑MS, **EI** is the gold standard. - For large biomolecules in LC‑MS, **ESI** is usually the best choice. - For imaging or rapid screening of large biomolecules, **MALDI** wins. - For non‑polar aromatics in LC‑MS, **APPI** is often superior. If you give me more details about your sample type, instrument, and analytical goals, I can narrow down the recommendation even further!
